Orientation, current state with the numbers to health-check against, the
remaining tracker phases, and how to run and verify.

The bulk of it is the invariants section: every entry there is a bug that
was found by running against live data and would be reintroduced by
someone reading only the code. The one that matters most is that fit and
pipeline are different axes -- an employer's rejection must never train
the ranker, or it learns to avoid the roles he most wanted.

Also records that agent-data's git history still holds the plaintext the
last commit stripped, and that squashing the branch would erase it.

the seen_jobs join that exposed the application history

applied.json and rejected.json are keyed by job id and were described as
holding "only opaque ids". seen_jobs.json sat on the same public branch
publishing title, company and url against those same ids, so a two-file
join resolved all nine applications to real postings -- Netflix, Portless,
A.Team and the rest -- readable by anyone, including a current employer.

seen_jobs.json now stores the opaque role_key instead of the plaintext it
was derived from, which is the only thing feedback.py ever read those
fields for. Existing entries are purged in place on the next run rather
than waiting out the 14-day expiry.

The docstrings claiming this made the history private are corrected rather
than left to overstate: the ids are sha1(posting URL), so re-fetching the
same public ATS boards and hashing still tests membership. Closing that
means moving the state off the public branch -- TRACKER_PLAN.md phase 0.

Design doc only, nothing built. Records the decisions made: public site
with private application history, batched-email write path, full pipeline
board.

Leads with the finding that shapes it -- applied.json's "opaque ids" are
trivially joined to seen_jobs.json on the same public branch, so the
current privacy claim in applied.py and rejected.py is false and the
whole application history is readable today.

Also fixes the axis that must not be merged: rejected.json is the owner's
"I don't want this" and trains the ranker; an employer's rejection must
not, or the ranker learns to avoid the roles he wanted most.

for $300k: location becomes a preference with a price

Remote stays the default requirement, but a role paying
RELOCATION_SALARY_USD or more is worth moving for, so above that figure
location stops filtering. Only ever against a *stated* salary -- an
on-site role that will not say what it pays cannot clear a bar it never
names. Those roles carry a banner in the digest, because "this one means
moving" must never be something you discover late.

Pay and location can no longer be separate gates, since each now decides
the other, so they are one step with the salary parsed first.

Three bugs surfaced getting there, each hiding the next:

us_friendly() only ever recognised remote-style strings ("Remote - US").
An on-site posting says "San Francisco, CA" -- no US token anywhere -- so
every US on-site role was being discarded as foreign. looks_us() reads
concrete locations, accepts a multi-office posting if any office is
American, and rejects the international ones by country or city.

_from_ats() passed remote=True as a positional literal, harmless while
every source was remote-only. It meant on-site roles arrived labelled
remote and were judged against the $130k bar instead of $300k -- SF jobs
presented as remote ones.

_relocation_grade() ran salary_max_usd() over raw prose, which returns the
largest number it can find, so "500,000 customers" or a $70B portfolio
read as relocation-grade pay and admitted ~180 roles that had no such
salary. Prose now goes through find_salary_snippet, which validates the
figure looks like compensation.

Greenhouse switched to content=true: one request per board instead of one
per posting, which is both politer and the only way to read pay, since it
publishes no structured compensation field. Salary is parsed there from
the untruncated text, because these postings put compensation at the very
bottom.

215 live roles, of which 90 are relocation-grade.

answers: cover the ~8-in-10 questions that never change

Across eight real Greenhouse forms, 52 questions needed answering and 36
were distinct by wording -- but that count is phrasing, not substance. One
question appears in five costumes ("will you require sponsorship", "do you
require immigration sponsorship", "will you now or at any time in the
future require visa sponsorship"...). Grouped by meaning, most questions
are standing facts that never change between applications.

standing_answers.py resolves them semantically, and resolves against the
field's actual shape: a select only accepts its own options, so each rule
carries a pattern for picking one. Where no option is true -- a "How did
you hear about us?" dropdown offering only Career Page / LinkedIn / Indeed
-- the question is handed back rather than answered wrongly. Option
matching had to learn real phrasings too: Affirm writes "No" as "I have
not previously been employed at Affirm".

Hard-coded per the owner: never requires sponsorship, authorized in the
US, no non-compete, not a government official, no prior employment at any
surfaced company. Deliberately NOT answered: arbitration and privacy
consent (accepting a legal agreement), and EEO, pronouns and "how do you
use AI tools" (self-identification). Those stay human.

Blocker detection now keys on the question stem rather than option count.
"Are you currently located within 50 miles of one of the locations listed
below?" lists six cities, so a count-based rule suppressed a genuine
on-site requirement, while "Which U.S. State do you reside in?" merely
records an address. Are you / Do you asks whether you qualify; Which /
What asks where you live.

The digest prints standing answers once instead of per card, and each job
now shows only what is genuinely left: 73% of answerable questions
resolve automatically, leaving two to five per application.

stop flagging records questions as blockers

Two false positives in the first live run. "Are you at least 18 years of
age?" was read as an 18-year experience requirement, and "What location
are you based in? (city, state, and country)" as an on-site requirement.
Three of five forms came back flagged, which would have taught the reader
to ignore the flag -- the same alert-fatigue failure the resume describes
fixing.

What separates a real screener is its shape, not its wording: a
disqualifier names one place and offers yes/no. So a location blocker now
requires a binary select. A fifty-item state dropdown and a free-text
location box are records questions and no longer flag. Years figures only
count when the question is about experience and not about age.

Cached verdicts carry an analysis version so a rules change re-evaluates
them rather than replaying yesterday's mistakes.

projects section; application pre-flight from the Greenhouse form

Resume
------
Added Selected Projects: the career agent (public, with stack) and
data-czars as an engineering artifact. The agent indexes GitHub but a
human reading the PDF saw nothing but the word "GitHub" in the header --
the strongest evidence for the AI-leaning half of the search was
invisible. The data-czars experience bullet gives up its module list to
the project entry and keeps the outcomes, so neither repeats the other.

Reframed the AI bullet around the constraint engineering that was the
actual substance: "researched and evaluated ... delivered demonstrations"
claimed no outcome at all, in the role that most needs one. Collapsed
four REST API bullets describing one achievement into two, dropped
fraternity memberships at four years' experience, and added remote
availability to the contact line since every targeted role is remote.

Pre-flight
----------
Greenhouse publishes a posting's full question set read-only at
?questions=true, and postings carry required screeners the job text never
mentions. A role that had cleared every remote filter here asks "Are you
based in, or very close to, Las Vegas, Nevada?" -- an evening of
form-filling wasted, discovered at the end.

preflight.py reads that form for each digest finalist, flags likely
blockers, and pre-fills the deterministic answers (9 of 22 on that
posting), including a standing answer to "how did you hear about us"
that names the agent itself. Free-text answers are deliberately NOT
drafted: a model-written "why do you want to work here" is the clearest
tell of a mass application, and considered applications are the whole
advantage here. Listing those questions early is the useful part.

Location screeners are only treated as blockers when they name one place
and want yes/no -- "Which U.S. State do you reside in?" is a records
question with a fifty-item dropdown, and flagged as a blocker at first.

Greenhouse jobs now carry their board token so the form is reachable even
when the posting URL points at the employer's own careers page. Nothing
is ever submitted: that endpoint requires the employer's API key and
answers 401 without it.

of 15, with up to 5 employer-direct roles at undisclosed pay

Dropping every posting without stated compensation was the largest single
loss in the funnel, and most of it was employers who publish through
their own ATS and simply withhold pay. Those now get a capped number of
slots -- but salary becomes the only unknown about them, so nothing else
is permitted to be:

  employer-direct    aggregator copies do not qualify
  posted within 14d  an old listing with no pay data is exactly where
                     "employer-direct" stops being reassuring
  80+ match, 0.7+ confidence, and a seniority verdict of target or
                     stretch -- a role that is reachable AND a real step
                     up, not a lateral move that happens to rank well

They are capped at 5 of 15 and can never displace a role that states what
it pays: selection walks the ranked list and skips over-quota entries
rather than truncating. Heuristic scores carry no seniority verdict, so
without a working LLM this fails closed and admits none of them.

Cards mark them "pay undisclosed" and "posted <14d - verify pay" so they
are never mistaken for a stated figure.

Timestamps needed real parsing for this: sources emit ISO with Z, ISO
with offset, date-only, and -- Lever -- epoch milliseconds, which naive
ISO parsing silently rejects. An unparseable date counts as too old.

drop the Domain skills section

The owner does not sit in a vertical -- the work has been enterprise-wide
across teams and asset classes throughout, so a section claiming banking
sub-domains as a specialism misrepresented the career and led with the
most dated material on the page.

Agentic & RAG Architecture moved to Process Optimization & Automation
rather than going with it: it is neither dated nor vertical, it is the
growth area, and it reinforces the automation narrative. CECL, SR 11-7,
mainframe migration and pricing remain in the experience bullets, where
they read as evidence rather than as a claimed specialism.

handle the /search-v2 response shape

/search returned `data` as a bare array; /search-v2 returns it as an
object holding `jobs` plus a pagination `cursor`. Iterating `data` gave
the dict's string keys, so every posting died on "'str' object has no
attribute 'get'" and the source contributed nothing despite finally
returning 200. Both shapes are handled, and the result fields are logged

# play-sports

AI-driven, physics-based football game project scaffold for Unreal Engine 5.

## Project Structure

- `play-sports.uproject` - Unreal Engine project definition.
- `Source/PlaySports` - main game module.
- `Plugins/Autonomix` - AI editor bypass plugin stub for T3D injection and Python scripting.
- `Plugins/AgenticLink` - external agent bridge plugin stub.
- `Data` - external data assets and ingestion sources.

## Implemented Systems

- `PSPlayerAttributes` - player attribute `USTRUCT` for data tables.
- `PSPlaySimulation` - headless play simulation state machine.
- `PSDataIngestion` - JSON-to-DataTable ingestion utility.
- `PSScheduleEngine` - programmatic 18-week season schedule generator.
- `PSFunctionalGym` - starting point for automated functional tests.

## Agentic Workflow

This repo is set up to be worked on by multiple AI coding tools (Claude Code, Antigravity,
GitHub Copilot, and free-tier models like Ollama/Gemini/OpenRouter) with shared context. See
[`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) for the architecture map, conventions, and how each tool's connectors
are wired up.

## Roadmap

Development is tracked in [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md): a 25-Epic core across 5 phases, sequenced
vertical-slice first (one crude but complete play end-to-end, then deepen each system), plus 100
expansion Epics (26–125) in themed track files under [`roadmap/`](roadmap/) — broadcast overlays,
cameras, stadium atmosphere, animation depth, gameplay nuance, AI, franchise, audio, UX,
multiplayer, engineering infrastructure, and content generation. Each expansion Epic is sized
(S/M/L/XL) and moded (code/editor/mixed) for agent scoping.

character archetypes, hitpoints, and combat rules (Epics 139-141)

Introduces the proprietary combat layer requested for future multiplayer
support: every on-field player has hitpoints (UPSHealthComponent +
UPSCombatRulesModel's deterministic damage rolls), a tackle no longer
unconditionally ends the play -- it deals damage, and the play only ends
once the ball carrier is downed. Downed carriers sit out exactly the next
play; non-carriers respawn at full health immediately (UPSRoster's new
FPSPlayerLiveState, extending its existing player-availability authority).
Interceptions auto-kill the QB's intended receiver rather than whoever the
ball hits. Punting is disallowed and the defense fields an extra player on
4th down (UPSRulesConfig). Player leveling/XP (UPSPlayerLeveling) grows
per-archetype attributes as a future microtransaction seam, gameplay only.

Also documents Track Q (roadmap/character-combat.md, Epics 139-141), a
recommended MVP priority sequencing across the code-mode expansion tracks
in ROADMAP.md, and answers (in the accompanying plan) why Epic 22's
animation work can't proceed without a human- or bridge-driven Editor

generalized data ingestion, validation, sample league (Epic 21)

Fixes a compile break in the previous commit (UFUNCTION inside a
USTRUCT is invalid -- FPSTeamStanding::GetWinPercentage() is now a
plain inline method).

UPSDataIngestion generalized beyond players: LoadTeamsFromJson,
LoadLeagueConfigFromJson (FPSLeagueConfig), plus
ValidatePlayersJson/ValidateTeamsJson returning "Row N: <field>
<problem>" actionable errors (missing PlayerId, unrecognized Role
enum string, negative numeric attributes, duplicate/missing TeamId).
UPSContentReimportCommandlet re-imports and validates every Data/
file in one action. Sample league dataset: 4 teams (Falcons + new
Hawks/Wolves/Bears rosters, ~11 players each covering every
EPlayerRole) plus sample_league_config.json. Data/README.md documents
the full contract for external tools/agents authoring content.

AI controller state authoritative in-memory; add Season/Franchise (Epic 20)

The previous fix (constructor-time Blackboard component) made the
component non-null but BB->InitializeBlackboard() on the dynamically-
synthesized UBlackboardData still returns false on this engine build
(root cause not identified without editor/debugger access -- flagged
for follow-up once real .uasset BlackboardData can be authored in
editor). Rather than keep guessing at engine internals blind,
APSOffenseController/APSDefenseController now treat plain in-memory
members as the authoritative state (CurrentPlayPhaseValue,
bHasPossessionValue, RouteWaypoints/CurrentWaypointIndex,
CurrentAssignment) with new BlueprintPure getters; the Blackboard
writes remain as a best-effort mirror for future editor-authored BT
assets but nothing depends on them succeeding. Updated all AI tests
to assert against the getters instead of raw Blackboard reads.

Epic 20: UPSFranchiseSeason (round-robin matchup generation over
UPSScheduleEngine's weeks, standings tracking), UPSQuickSimRunner
(drives UPSPlaySimulation's existing quick-sim rolls headlessly to a
final score, reusing it as the single authority on play outcomes
rather than duplicating scoring logic), UPSPlayoffBracket (seeded
single-elimination bracket from final standings), UPSFranchiseSaveGame
(persists season state through the existing UPSSaveSubsystem).

pre-existing Blackboard init failure; add roster/progression/injury (Epic 19)

Root-cause fix: APSOffenseController/APSDefenseController lazily created
their Blackboard component via UseBlackboard() inside OnPossess. In
headless/automation-test worlds that runtime-created component is never
registered, so UseBlackboard() silently fails and every key resolves to
KeyID 65535 (invalid) -- this was failing
PlaySports.AI.OffenseControllerTelemetrySync on every CI run back to
2deebdc, before this session's changes, and newly broke my Epic 15/17
tests that inherited the same pattern. Fix: create the Blackboard
component as a constructor-time CreateDefaultSubobject (the standard
AIController idiom) so it's always registered when the actor spawns,
and call BB->InitializeBlackboard() directly.

Epic 19: UPSRoster (53-player roster + ordered depth chart per role,
fatigue-driven backup substitution reading the Epic 6 stamina hooks),
UPSPlayerProgression (age-curve growth/decline, data-driven via
FPSProgressionTuning), UPSInjuryModel (fatigue-scaled per-play injury
probability/severity, seedable for replay). FPSPersonnelPackage data
shape defined but not yet wired to formation resolution -- left
unchecked on the roadmap.

coaching & play-selection AI (Epic 18)

UPSCoachingAI weights play categories from an FPSSituationContext
(down/distance/clock/score) and a data-driven FPSTendencyProfile
(aggression + per-category weight table), then weighted-randomly
selects among matching plays with a seedable RandomStream for
deterministic replay. 4th-down, 2-point, and clock-management
decision helpers. IPSCoachingSuggestionProvider is a designed-but-
unimplemented LLM hook -- gated behind the AgenticLink bridge
(Plugins/AgenticLink is still a stub), falls back to internal
weighting when no provider is registered. PlayCategory field added
to FPSPlayDefinition and populated across the starter playbook.

22-agent play orchestration and route-waypoint API (Epic 17)

UPSPlayOrchestrator distributes a selected FPSPlayDefinition into
per-pawn route/coverage assignments across all on-field pawns, role
by role, deduplicating repeated role slots. Adds
APSOffenseController::SetAssignedRoute/AdvanceToNextWaypoint (Target
Location + RouteWaypointIndex blackboard keys per the offense AI
spec) so the orchestrator has a real API to drive. Scramble-drill
broken-play adaptation and a seedable FRandomStream for deterministic

Extracts the Reverb's actual DSP engine into a new JUCE-free ReverbCore
class, so it can eventually be hosted by something other than JUCE/
APVTS -- specifically the future LPI-ABI wrapper (Epic B, #97).
LoudioReverbProcessor thins down to exactly two bridges: APVTS<->
ReverbCore parameter sync each block, and ReverbCore's analyzer output
-> dspToUiRingBuffer. Every formula in ReverbCore::process() is a
line-for-line port of the pre-extraction processBlock(), cross-checked
directly against the prior commit's source.

Three JUCE-free replacements, following the existing stb_truetype.h
single-header-vendoring precedent (Plugins/Reverb/
ARCHITECTURE_DECISIONS.md #2) where a from-scratch implementation was
the more self-contained/auditable choice over vendoring an unverified
third-party dependency:
- SimpleFFT: standard radix-2 Cooley-Tukey complex FFT (juce::dsp::FFT
  replacement). Not real-only optimized, but at 1024 points once per
  UI-refresh-rate-ish cadence this is not remotely a bottleneck.
- SimpleBiquad: RBJ Audio EQ Cookbook shelf/peak formulas
  (juce::dsp::IIR::Coefficients replacement), the well-established
  public reference JUCE's own coefficient generation closely follows.
- SimpleSmoothedValue: linear ramp smoothing (juce::LinearSmoothedValue
  replacement), identical semantics.

New shared parameter table (SharedStructures.h's kReverbParams[]) is
the single source of truth for every parameter's id/name/range/
default/step -- both createParameterLayout() and ReverbCore now read
from it, so the numbers can't independently drift. Cross-checked every
single value against the prior commit's hardcoded createParameterLayout()
by direct diff, confirming byte-for-byte identical parameter ids,
ranges, steps, and defaults -- APVTS's XML serialization format (and
therefore existing preset/session compatibility) is unchanged by
construction, not just by assumption.

ReverbCore exposes two ways to set a parameter, matching two genuinely
different threading situations: setParameterValueDirect() (same-thread,
immediate -- what the JUCE wrapper uses every block, since it already
has APVTS as a thread-safe value source) and setParameterValue()
(RT-safe, ring-buffered, matching the LPI ABI's set_parameter_value
contract exactly -- unused by the JUCE path today, ready for the
future LPI wrapper). getState()/setState() is a separate small binary
blob for a host with no APVTS-equivalent preset mechanism at all;
LoudioReverbProcessor's own getStateInformation/setStateInformation
keep using APVTS's existing XML shape completely unchanged.

Scope note: this issue's plan also described extracting PluginEditor.
cpp's widget-construction code behind a shared ParamBridge abstraction,
for the JUCE wrapper and a future LPI offscreen GUI to both reuse.
Deferred to B4 (#101) instead of done speculatively here -- B4 is where
a real second consumer (the LPI GUI) will actually exist to design
that abstraction against, rather than guessing its shape now with
nothing to verify it against.

9 new tests in DSPTests.cpp (18/18 total) exercising ReverbCore
directly: param table index integrity, defaults match the shared
table, both parameter-set paths (immediate and ring-buffered), a
zero-tolerance dryWet=0.0 bit-exact passthrough check, white-noise
stability (finite/bounded over 8192 samples), freeze-mode tail-energy
sustain, state save/load round-trip, and analyzer dirty-flag lifecycle.

Verified: full dsp_tests (18/18) and a real Standalone rebuild --
PID-verified screenshots confirm default parameter values match the
shared table exactly, a real WM_LBUTTONDOWN/MOUSEMOVE/UP drag on the
Decay Time knob correctly changes its value (0.11 -> 0.41) end-to-end
through the ring-buffer -> APVTS -> ReverbCore path, and all 10
Advanced-tab knobs (post-EQ, crossover, ducking, gating -- all now
SimpleBiquad/ReverbCore-backed) render correctly.

Found and fixed two build issues along the way: a name collision with
juce::SmoothedValue (renamed to SimpleSmoothedValue, matching the
Simple* naming already established by SimpleBiquad/SimpleFFT), and
windows.h's min/max macros (pulled in transitively via cuif/
ring_buffer.h) clashing with std::max/std::min in the gate-fade clamp
(replaced with plain conditionals).

Louard","email":"mbf.louard@gmail.com","date":"2026-07-18T11:33:26Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-18T11:33:26Z"},"message":"B2: cuif offscreen rendering mode (#108)

Extends cuif_window with an offscreen render path -- a new
cuif_window_create_offscreen() creates a hidden HWND (same "backing
window nobody ever sees" trick already used to bootstrap the
process-wide root GL context) whose GL context targets an FBO-backed
RGBA8 color texture instead of that HWND's own on-screen framebuffer.
cuif_window_render_frame() renders into it exactly as normal (widget/
graphics code never touches window->hwnd/hdc directly, so it's
completely unaware of the distinction); cuif_window_read_pixels()
reads the result back instead of a real window ever presenting
anything via SwapBuffers.

New cuif_window_inject_mouse_down/up/move() call the exact same
cuif_widget_dispatch_mouse_*() functions cuif_wnd_proc() calls for
real WM_LBUTTONDOWN/UP/WM_MOUSEMOVE messages, just without an actual
Win32 message ever being sent -- this is the synthetic input path a
future frame-streaming input relay (browser-forwarded mouse events)
will call into.

MSAA is not requested for offscreen windows in this version (FBO
multisample-resolve is unimplemented) -- cuif's adaptive tessellation
already reduces aliasing enough that this is a reasonable v1 scope
cut. FBO functions (glGenFramebuffers etc., GL 3.0 core /
ARB_framebuffer_object) are resolved via wglGetProcAddress, same
pattern already used for MSAA and glGenerateMipmap resolution
elsewhere in this file.

Intended for hosts with no native window surface to embed into (e.g.
noprod's browser-based UI) -- see Plugins/Reverb/
ARCHITECTURE_DECISIONS.md and Epic B (LPI).

New standalone test harness (offscreen_harness.c, since there's no
visible window to screenshot the normal way): builds a knob widget,
renders a frame, injects a real synthetic drag (down + 20 move steps
+ up), renders again, dumps both frames to disk as BMP. Visually
confirmed: knob value climbs from 0.30 to 0.60 exactly matching the
drag, text renders crisp at 1.5x DPI. Caught and fixed two real
ordering bugs along the way while building this harness: (1) loading
the font before the window/GL context existed (the same class of
context-timing bug fixed elsewhere in this codebase -- must load
after the window makes its context current), (2) needing the same
DPI rebake step PluginEditor.cpp already does, without which text
renders at the wrong effective resolution for a non-1.0x scale.

3 new automated tests in cuif_tests.c (28/28 total): FBO render +
read_pixels() returns the correct theme background color,
read_pixels() rejects an undersized buffer and a non-offscreen
window, and injected mouse input reaches a widget's callback
identically to a real WM_LBUTTONDOWN.

Verified: full cuif_tests (28/28) and dsp_tests (9/9) suites pass;
Standalone rebuilt and screenshot-verified with no visual regression

B2: cuif offscreen rendering mode (#108)

Extends cuif_window with an offscreen render path -- a new
cuif_window_create_offscreen() creates a hidden HWND (same "backing
window nobody ever sees" trick already used to bootstrap the
process-wide root GL context) whose GL context targets an FBO-backed
RGBA8 color texture instead of that HWND's own on-screen framebuffer.
cuif_window_render_frame() renders into it exactly as normal (widget/
graphics code never touches window->hwnd/hdc directly, so it's
completely unaware of the distinction); cuif_window_read_pixels()
reads the result back instead of a real window ever presenting
anything via SwapBuffers.

New cuif_window_inject_mouse_down/up/move() call the exact same
cuif_widget_dispatch_mouse_*() functions cuif_wnd_proc() calls for
real WM_LBUTTONDOWN/UP/WM_MOUSEMOVE messages, just without an actual
Win32 message ever being sent -- this is the synthetic input path a
future frame-streaming input relay (browser-forwarded mouse events)
will call into.

MSAA is not requested for offscreen windows in this version (FBO
multisample-resolve is unimplemented) -- cuif's adaptive tessellation
already reduces aliasing enough that this is a reasonable v1 scope
cut. FBO functions (glGenFramebuffers etc., GL 3.0 core /
ARB_framebuffer_object) are resolved via wglGetProcAddress, same
pattern already used for MSAA and glGenerateMipmap resolution
elsewhere in this file.

Intended for hosts with no native window surface to embed into (e.g.
noprod's browser-based UI) -- see Plugins/Reverb/
ARCHITECTURE_DECISIONS.md and Epic B (LPI).

New standalone test harness (offscreen_harness.c, since there's no
visible window to screenshot the normal way): builds a knob widget,
renders a frame, injects a real synthetic drag (down + 20 move steps
+ up), renders again, dumps both frames to disk as BMP. Visually
confirmed: knob value climbs from 0.30 to 0.60 exactly matching the
drag, text renders crisp at 1.5x DPI. Caught and fixed two real
ordering bugs along the way while building this harness: (1) loading
the font before the window/GL context existed (the same class of
context-timing bug fixed elsewhere in this codebase -- must load
after the window makes its context current), (2) needing the same
DPI rebake step PluginEditor.cpp already does, without which text
renders at the wrong effective resolution for a non-1.0x scale.

3 new automated tests in cuif_tests.c (28/28 total): FBO render +
read_pixels() returns the correct theme background color,
read_pixels() rejects an undersized buffer and a non-offscreen
window, and injected mouse input reaches a widget's callback
identically to a real WM_LBUTTONDOWN.

Verified: full cuif_tests (28/28) and dsp_tests (9/9) suites pass;
Standalone rebuilt and screenshot-verified with no visual regression
(this touches window_win32.c, shared with the VST3/Standalone build).

since it's out of this issue's scope.

contention).

cuif_global_font was never reset to NULL when the last window closed,
even though its GL texture was destroyed along with that window's
context. On reopen, ensureCuifWindowCreated()'s "already loaded" guard
saw a non-NULL pointer and skipped reloading the font, so it bound a

Fix cuif_global_font lifecycle (reopen-in-place fix) (#103)

cuif_global_font was never reset to NULL when the last window closed,
even though its GL texture was destroyed along with that window's
context. On reopen, ensureCuifWindowCreated()'s "already loaded" guard
saw a non-NULL pointer and skipped reloading the font, so it bound a
texture_id that no longer existed in the new context -- the same
dangling-texture symptom as #88, just triggered by a single instance's
close/reopen cycle instead of two simultaneous instances.

Frees the font and resets the pointer inside the same cuif_window_count
== 0 teardown block introduced in #91/#102, so it's only ever alive
while at least one window exists anywhere in the process. The root
context is made current just for the glDeleteTextures() call, since by
this point the window that brought the count to zero already had its
own context deleted.

New automated test drives the exact mechanism the plugin editor's guard
relies on: cuif_global_font must be NULL once zero windows exist.

  visibly wrong. Now uses real glyph advance metrics.

  frame. cuif_font_load() runs before any window's first render call,

  current at all (undefined behavior that happened to be silently
  tolerated by this driver rather than a guarantee) -- found while
  investigating where to hook the new mipmap-generation extension
  resolution.

  texture isn't valid across multiple plugin instances' independent,
  unshared GL contexts -- a pre-existing architectural gap surfaced
  while rewriting this file, needs wglShareLists or a per-window atlas.

"Advanced", "Pre-Delay", "Damping"), a dramatic change from the
illegible blur in every earlier screenshot this epic started from.

- cuif_draw_bezier (its curve-flattening loop now fills a point array

  GL_LINE_STRIP + glLineWidth(3.0f) that bypassed every shared helper)

  glLineWidth(2.0f))

Also lands the arc-point-generation consolidation deferred from #81:
new cuif_generate_arc_points() (graphics.h/graphics.c) is now the
single source of adaptively-tessellated arc points, used by both
cuif_draw_rounded_rect's corners and draw_arc's stroke -- draw_arc no
longer has its own copy of the angle-stepping loop.

Verified: 20/20 cuif_tests pass (adds a geometry-correctness test for
cuif_generate_arc_points: start/end points land exactly on the
requested angles, every generated point lies on the circle). Built
VST3/Standalone/dsp_tests clean. Screenshotted the Standalone build
zoomed on a knob and the bezier curve -- clean, consistent-thickness
strokes with no gaps or artifacts. Dragged a bezier node to create a
real angled joint (not just a flat line) and re-screenshotted -- the
bevel joins hold up correctly through actual curvature, not just the
degenerate flat case. Sent real interaction (tab switch, node drag)
throughout; process stayed responsive.

Louard","email":"mbf.louard@gmail.com","date":"2026-07-17T14:13:07Z"},"committer":{"name":"GitHub","email":"noreply@github.com","date":"2026-07-17T14:13:07Z"},"message":"Add adaptive tessellation for arcs and rounded-rect corners (#81) (#86)

Root cause #2 of the rendering-quality overhaul, and the direct cause
of the "octagonal knobs" complaint: cuif_draw_rounded_rect hardcoded
8 segments/corner (graphics.c) and widget.c's draw_arc hardcoded 32
segments/circle (used for every knob's track/value arc) regardless of
actual on-screen radius.

New cuif_arc_segment_count(radius_px, sweep_radians) in
Framework/include/cuif/tessellation.h: a chord-error-bounded formula
(the standard approach in vector renderers like Skia/NanoVG) instead
of a fixed guess. radius_px must be in DEVICE pixels
(logical_radius * dpi_scale, from #79) -- this is what makes
tessellation scale up correctly on high-DPI displays instead of the
fixed counts this replaces getting proportionally *more* faceted as
physical pixel density increases.

Tuning note: an initial 0.25px chord-error tolerance actually produced
*fewer* segments than the old fixed 32 at real knob sizes (25 vs 32
at a 70x70 knob's ~22px radius) -- a regression at today's normal 1x
scale, the exact resolution the original complaint was reported at.
Tightened to 0.05px so both the 1x and 2x cases clearly exceed the old
baseline (36 and 50 segments respectively for a 70x70 knob).
Encoded as an explicit test assertion so this can't regress silently
again.

Both cuif_draw_rounded_rect and draw_arc pull the active window's
dpi_scale via the existing cuif_current_window global + the #79
cuif_window_get_dpi_scale() accessor -- no signature changes needed.

Deliberately deferred: consolidating emit_arc (graphics.c) and
draw_arc (widget.c) into one shared arc-point-generation helper, since
#82 needs arc points as an ordered polyline for quad-based stroke
rendering anyway -- doing that consolidation now would mean
re-refactoring it again immediately after for #82's actual shape
requirements.

Verified: 19/19 cuif_tests pass (adds 3 tessellation tests: monotonic
with radius, clamped at floor/ceiling, and the regression test above).
Built cuif_harness/VST3/Standalone/dsp_tests clean. Screenshotted the
Standalone build before/after (zoomed on the hero knob) -- faceting is
visibly gone. Sent a real tab-switch click post-change to confirm
interaction still works; process stayed responsive throughout.

# Background
## Professionally
I work in banking, which is largely why none of my analytical toolset can be displayed here. Recently migrated Unsecured Installment loans from a legacy mainframe to one we own, so I have skills, you'll just have to trust me :). 
I'm a business analytics consultant, but that means nothing anymore. I optimize processes. I believe everyone always has, but now I do it very well, with the assist of agents. 
## Personally
I'm sort of obsessed with creating my own Digital Audio Workstation and every thing that goes into that. That work is available on my profile, and probably largely what gets contributed here for the time being. 
## Extras
Before AI I was a dreamer, now I am lazy if my dreams don't actually ship.

Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:55:28Z"},"committer":{"name":"Michael Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:55:28Z"},"message":"Make VST folder scan real: enumerate and persist actual plugins (#26)

Replaces the fake "Rescanning... Complete!" alert with a real scan:
the user picks a folder via the File System Access API and the app
recursively enumerates actual plugin binaries (.vst3/.dll/.clap/
.component), recording name, format, and path. The discovered list
persists in localStorage across sessions, de-duplicates by path, and
each plugin can be added to the selected track's device chain
(carrying its pluginPath for future native hosting). Remaining for
#26: loading scanned plugins in Audio Core (JUCE) for actual DSP —
audio_core scans VST3s at startup but doesn't yet expose hosting over

controls (closes #36)

A punch strip sits atop the arrangement timeline: drag to set the
punch region (snapped to beats), with a PUNCH toggle in the transport.
While playback runs with punch enabled, the playhead loop engages the
record state when crossing the punch-in point and disengages it at
punch-out, so recording no longer depends on manually timing the
record button. (Recording itself remains the app's arm/record state —
actual audio input capture is a separate future feature.)

Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:47:06Z"},"committer":{"name":"Michael Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:47:06Z"},"message":"Add audio warping: transient detection + granular time-stretch (closes #17)

Enabling Warp in Clip View runs energy-based transient detection on
the clip and estimates its native tempo from the median transient
interval (folded into 70-180 BPM). Warped clips render at their
tempo-stretched length with transient markers overlaid, and play back
through a granular overlap-add scheduler (90ms grains, 50% crossfade)
so they follow the project tempo without repitching. Changing the
project BPM re-stretches warped clips both visually and audibly.
Warp mode (Beats/Tones/Texture) and original BPM are editable per clip.

Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:42:11Z"},"committer":{"name":"Michael Louard","email":"mbl63@case.edu","date":"2026-07-16T22:42:11Z"},"message":"Add track freeze & flatten via offline rendering (closes #29)

Freeze renders a track's clips through an OfflineAudioContext (MIDI
notes are rendered through the track's synth instrument; audio clips
with their trim/offset) and stores the buffer on the track. While
frozen: playback uses the rendered buffer instead of live clips, and
the device chain panel is locked with a Frozen banner. Flatten
permanently replaces the track's clips, instrument, and devices with
the frozen audio and converts the track to an audio track. Both are
undoable. Note: chain effects are still UI-only (no DSP until
#18-#21), so renders cover instrument + clip audio.

mappings and presets (closes #22)

Racks are container devices in a track's chain holding nested devices
plus four macro knobs. Each macro carries mappings (device, parameter,
min..max); sweeping the macro drives every mapped parameter across its
range. Devices can be grouped into a rack ("Group into Rack" wraps the
track's loose devices), added/removed inside the rack, and racks can
be saved as presets and instantiated on any track (deep-cloned with
fresh ids and remapped macro targets).

tracks with summing (closes #28)

Group tracks now fold/unfold via a chevron (members hide from the
arranger, mixer headers, and session view while their audio keeps
playing), show a member count, and get a purple-tinted header. The
audio graph now honors grouping: member track gains are patched into
the group track's gain node (true summing bus, so group volume/mute
affects all members) instead of every track connecting straight to
master, with re-patching only when a track's routing target changes.
Also exposes the store on window.__dawStore in dev builds for
console/automation access.

# invincible-bot

Pulls files/attachments from channel `1220379903795531896` (guild `1218743328720556042`) using [DiscordChatExporter](https://github.com/Tyrrrz/DiscordChatExporter) (DCE).

We don't own/admin that server, so a bot can't be invited to it — DCE authenticates with your own **user token** instead, which works for any channel you can already see in the Discord client.

> Using a personal user token with a third-party tool is against Discord's ToS in the fine print. This is for personal archiving of a channel you're already a member of — don't use the token for anything else, don't share it, and don't run this against servers/channels you don't have a legitimate reason to access.

## Setup

1. **Download DiscordChatExporter CLI** (self-contained build, no .NET install required):
   - Go to https://github.com/Tyrrrz/DiscordChatExporter/releases/latest
   - Download `DiscordChatExporter.Cli.zip` (the CLI build, not the GUI)
   - Extract it into `tools/` in this repo, so you end up with `tools/DiscordChatExporter.Cli.exe`

2. **Get your Discord user token**:
   - Open Discord in a browser and log in
   - Open DevTools (F12) → Network tab → refresh the page
   - Click any request to `discord.com/api/...`, find the `authorization` request header, copy its value

3. Copy `.env.example` to `.env` and paste your token into `USER_AUTH_TOKEN`. Guild/channel IDs are already filled in.

## Usage

```powershell
./export.ps1
```

This exports the channel's messages to `exports/<channel-name>.html` and downloads every attachment into `exports/files/`.

Files are safe to re-run — DCE reuses already-downloaded media instead of re-fetching it.

# copilot-credit-tracker (`ccred`)

Track where your GitHub Copilot premium-request credits actually go — and whether the
model you picked earned them.

- **Start mid-cycle, not from zero.** `ccred import` pulls what you have already
  spent this month out of GitHub's billing data and into the ledger, so the first
  thing you see is your real number rather than an empty bar.
- **Burn rate first.** How much of the monthly allowance is gone, how fast, and what
  the projection says about the rest of the cycle.
- **Session shape.** One-prompt wins vs. five-prompt grinds, and the share of your
  spend that went to follow-ups instead of openers.
- **Prompt length.** Whether longer opening prompts actually buy fewer follow-ups.
- **Token dimensions.** Input, output and context tracked separately, and priced
  separately if your agreement bills that way.
- **Personal and enterprise.** The local ledger always works; `ccred sync` reconciles
  against GitHub's billing usage API for a personal account, an organization or an
  enterprise (including GHES base URLs). No API access? Import the CSV instead.

Zero runtime dependencies — Node built-ins only. Nothing to vendor, nothing to audit,
nothing to break an internal registry mirror.

---

## Install

```bash
npm link
```

From then on `ccred` works in any directory. To install from a private registry
instead:

```bash
npm install -g copilot-credit-tracker
```

Requires Node 18.17 or newer.

## Quick start

```bash
ccred init --plan pro --reset-day 14
```

`--reset-day` is the day of the month your Copilot allowance renews — for most
personal plans that is your subscription renewal date, not the 1st.

If the cycle is already underway, pull in what you have spent so far — the tracker
does not have to start at zero:

```bash
ccred import
```

Log a request as you make it:

```bash
ccred log sonnet "fix the auth redirect loop"
```

Follow-ups on the same problem join the same session automatically:

```bash
ccred p "still looping, here is the middleware"
ccred p "try guarding on the referrer"
ccred end --solved
```

Then look at the damage:

```bash
ccred
```


## A note on billing models

GitHub has two. The current platform bills **AI credits**, priced per token. The
legacy platform bills **premium requests**, priced by a per-model multiplier. The
Copilot CLI says so directly — `copilot help billing`: *"Usage is measured in AI
credits. If you're on the legacy billing platform, you may see premium requests
instead."*

`ccred` reads and reports both. `harvest` picks up whichever your CLI recorded, and
the per-model multiplier table only applies to the legacy unit.

## Starting mid-cycle

Installing this on the 20th should not mean pretending the month began on the 20th.
There are three ways to bring the cycle so far into the ledger, in order of how much
they ask of you.

### 1. Harvest the Copilot CLI (no token, no network, no permissions)

The Copilot CLI already records what every session cost, on your own machine, under
`~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/events.jsonl`. Reading it needs nothing but your home
directory:

```bash
ccred harvest
```

```
Harvested 2026-08 from the Copilot CLI
--------------------------------------
  source             ~/.copilot (no token, no network, no billing permission)
  sessions on disk   5 finished, 4 in this cycle
  added              3 sessions (12.95 AI credits, 46 premium requests)
  tokens             154.0k of conversation, read from the CLI's own record
  turn counts        2 sessions did not record how many prompts it took

  day         model              AI credits  prem reqs  turns  tokens
  ----------  -----------------  ----------  ---------  -----  ------
  2026-08-18  claude-sonnet-4.5         2.4         12      3   48.0k
  2026-08-20  claude-opus-4.1          9.75         30      -   91.0k
  2026-08-25  gpt-5                     0.8          4      -   15.0k
```

This is strictly better than the billing API: it carries **real token counts and AI
credits**, which billing does not report at all, plus real session boundaries, the
model, the branch and the lines changed. Sessions are keyed by the CLI's own session
id, so running it again adds nothing and picks up whatever has happened since.

What it does *not* give you is your plan's remaining balance — the CLI shows that in
its footer but does not pass it to integrations. Harvesting tells you what you have
spent, which is the number this tool is built around.

Point it elsewhere with `CCRED_COPILOT_HOME` if your CLI keeps state somewhere else.
Verified against Copilot CLI 1.0.81; every field is read defensively, so a CLI that
changes shape harvests nothing rather than writing wrong numbers.

### 2. Import from GitHub billing

If you have billing read access — an owner, a billing manager, or a personal account
— `ccred import` reads the billing usage API for the cycle and writes it in:

```bash
ccred import
```

```
Imported 2026-08 (Aug 14 - Sep 14)
----------------------------------
  source             GitHub billing usage (personal, gh auth token)
  added              62 credits over 3 days (35 premium requests, 4 models)
  unattributed       4 credits GitHub reported without naming a model
  tokens             not reported - GitHub bills per premium request, not per token

  ██████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ 62/300 21%
  was 0 before this import

  model                                 mult  credits  requests  days
  ------------------------------------  ----  -------  --------  ----
  Claude Opus 4.1                       x10        30         3    1d
  Claude Sonnet 4.5                     x1         21        21    2d
  GPT-5                                 x1          7         7    1d
  Premium request (model not reported)  x1          4         4    1d
```

Do it as part of setup with `ccred init --plan pro --reset-day 14 --import`, or any
time afterwards. Past cycles work too: `ccred import 2026-07` writes into that
cycle's archive.

### 3. If you are blocked from the billing API

Billing usage is an owner / billing-manager surface. A developer holding a Copilot
Business or Enterprise seat is exactly the person who wants this tool and exactly the
person most likely to get a `403` from that endpoint — and GitHub Enterprise Server or
an older account will return `404` instead. Neither failure is a reason to start from
zero, so there are two routes that never touch the API.

**Import a file.** If you can reach a usage report at all — a download from the billing
page, an export a colleague with billing access sent you — the file reader takes it:

```bash
ccred import --file ~/Downloads/usage-2026-08.csv
```

It takes GitHub's CSV export, the billing API's JSON response saved verbatim, or any
CSV with a date, a model or SKU, and a quantity. Headers are matched loosely, so
`Net Amount`, `netAmount` and `net_amount` are the same column, and a spreadsheet that
saved semicolons instead of commas still reads. If your file happens to carry token
counts, they come in too.

**Type the number in.** If all you can do is *read* a total off a screen — a usage
page with no export, a figure an admin quoted you — enter it directly:

```bash
ccred import --credits 142                      # a total
ccred import --credits opus=60,sonnet=33        # or split by model, if you know it
```

A hand-entered figure is treated as an **opening balance**, not a day's work: it is
dated to the first day of the cycle and can never show up as your busiest day. It
counts toward your budget, pace and projection, which is the whole point — you are
still spending against the same 300.

Check the number again in a week and re-run it. The same gap arithmetic applies, so
`--credits 160` after `--credits 142` adds 18, and running the same number twice
changes nothing. Splitting by model is optional; without it the credits land against
`Premium request (model not reported)` at 1×, which keeps the total honest even though
it cannot tell you which model earned it.

Both routes leave `ccred log` working exactly as before, so from the day you install,
new work carries the full session shape regardless of what your org lets you read.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--file <path>` | Import from a downloaded report instead of the API. |
| `--credits N` | Enter a total by hand as an opening balance. `--credits opus=60,sonnet=33` splits it by model. |
| `--dry-run` | Show exactly what would be added and write nothing. Still reads from GitHub. |
| `--replace` | Discard earlier backfills for the cycle and re-import, for when GitHub's report was revised or you imported the wrong scope. |
| `--clear` | Remove backfilled entries and keep everything you logged by hand. |
| `--quantity raw` | Read the quantity column as model interactions to be multiplied, rather than as already-billed premium requests. |
| `--scope` / `--org` / `--enterprise` / `--token` | Same as `ccred sync`. |

### Importing twice is safe

Import fills the gap rather than appending. For each day and model it compares
GitHub's number against what the ledger already holds and adds only the difference:

- Run it twice and the second run adds nothing.
- Log five Sonnet prompts today, then import a day GitHub billed at twelve, and seven
  credits are added — not twelve.
- Log more than GitHub reports and nothing is touched; the excess is shown as
  `ledger ahead` so you can go and find the mis-log.

### What a backfilled day can and cannot tell you

GitHub's billing data is a date, a SKU and a quantity. It does not say which prompts
belonged to the same problem, how long any of them were, or how many tokens moved —
GitHub bills per premium request, not per token, and reports no token counts at all.

So imported entries are marked, and the report keeps them in their place:

| | counts backfilled spend | logged prompts only |
| --- | --- | --- |
| credits, allowance, pace, projection | yes | |
| daily burn, per-model spend and share | yes | |
| sessions, one-and-done rate, re-prompt tax | | yes |
| prompt length and follow-ups by opener | | yes |
| credits per session, cost to finish | | yes |

That is the point of the split: a backfilled month can tell you truthfully what you
spent, and would only lie if it were allowed to tell you how you spent it. Everything
you log from the day you install carries the full picture.

## Commands

### Logging

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ccred log <model> [note]` | Log one premium request. Joins the open session if it is still warm, otherwise starts a new one. |
| `ccred start <model> [label]` | Open a session explicitly. |
| `ccred p [note]` | Log another prompt in the open session (same model unless you pass `--model`). |
| `ccred end [--solved\|--partial\|--wasted]` | Close the open session. The outcome is optional. |
| `ccred undo` | Drop the last logged prompt. |

Optional detail on any log command:

```
--text "…"      measure length from the prompt itself
--file p.md     …or from a file
--stdin         …or from a pipe:  cat prompt.md | ccred log opus --stdin
--chars N       …or state it directly
--words N
--in N --out N --ctx N     input / output / context tokens
--count N       more than one premium request in one go
--multiplier N  override the multiplier (also registers an unknown model)
--tag a,b       free-form tags
--solo          force a standalone one-prompt session
```

A session that has been idle for 45 minutes (configurable) will not swallow your next
prompt — a fresh one starts instead.

### Reporting

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ccred` / `ccred status` | Burn-rate summary for the live cycle. |
| `ccred report [cycle]` | Full analysis: burn, session shape, per-model efficiency, prompt length, tokens. |
| `ccred history [-n 12]` | Every cycle side by side. |
| `ccred export [cycle] --format csv --out usage.csv` | csv, json or ndjson; `--period all` for everything. |

`cycle` is an id like `2026-07`, or `current` / `last`.

Every command accepts `--json` for machine-readable output, so this composes with
whatever dashboard you already have.

### Setup

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ccred init --plan pro --reset-day 14` | Plan, allowance and cycle anchor. |
| `ccred config` | Show every setting. |
| `ccred config set <key> <value>` | Dotted keys, e.g. `github.enterprise`. |
| `ccred config path` | Where the data lives. |
| `ccred models` | Multipliers and plan allowances. |
| `ccred models --set claude-opus-4.1=10` | Correct a multiplier, or register a model GitHub added after this release. |
| `ccred harvest [cycle]` | Read the Copilot CLI's own session logs on this machine. No token needed. |
| `ccred sync` | Reconcile the ledger against GitHub's billing usage API. |
| `ccred import [cycle]` | Pull a cycle's spend out of GitHub and into the ledger. `--file <path>` reads a downloaded report instead. |

## How the monthly reset works

The live cycle lives in one file. Every command loads it and checks the clock first:

- If the reset day has passed, the finished cycle is written to
  `archive/<cycle-id>.json` and a fresh empty cycle takes its place.
- Any session still open at the boundary is closed **at** the boundary, so work never
  straddles two cycles.
- Several missed cycles roll over in one go — the tool catches up whenever you next
  run it, even if that is three months later.
- A cycle with nothing in it is not archived; an absent file simply means a quiet month.
- Archives are never rewritten by the live cycle, so last month's numbers stay exactly
  as they were.

There is no cron job, no daemon and nothing to remember. Reset day 31 clamps to the
last day of shorter months, and because exactly one cycle begins in each calendar
month, cycle ids stay unique whatever anchor you pick.

Changing `plan` or `allowance` applies to the live cycle immediately. Changing
`cycleResetDay` re-anchors the current cycle without losing what is already logged.

## Where the data lives

Outside this repo and outside your working directory, so it survives across shells,
terminals and projects:

| Platform | Path |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\copilot-credit-tracker\` |
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/copilot-credit-tracker/` |
| Linux | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/copilot-credit-tracker/` (or `~/.local/share/…`) |

```
config.json            settings
current.json           the live cycle
archive/2026-07.json   finished cycles, one file each
models.override.json   your multiplier corrections
```

Set `CCRED_HOME` to point somewhere else — the clean way to keep a work profile
separate from a personal one:

```bash
CCRED_HOME=~/.ccred-work ccred status
```

Writes are atomic (temp file plus rename), so an interrupted command cannot leave a
truncated ledger.

## What the efficiency numbers mean

**Re-prompt tax** — the share of your credits spent on prompts *after* the opening one.
A high number means you are paying repeatedly to explain the same problem.

**Credits per session** — the honest cost of finishing something. Only sessions run
entirely on one model count toward that model's figure, so a mixed session cannot
flatter either model. This is the number that answers "is Opus at 10× worth it": a
model that resolves in one prompt at 10× beats one that needs six at 1×.

**Follow-ups by opener length** — sessions bucketed by how long their *first* prompt
was, against how many extra prompts they went on to need. If the terse bucket needs
three follow-ups and the detailed bucket needs none, that is worth knowing.

**Token dimensions** — input, output and context are recorded per prompt and totalled
per model. GitHub bills per premium request rather than per token, so these are
informational by default. If your agreement does price tokens, set the rates and they
are folded into the credit totals:

```bash
ccred config set tokenRates.default.input 0.5    # credits per 1k tokens
ccred config set tokenRates.default.output 1.5
```

## Syncing with GitHub (personal and enterprise)

`sync` and `import` read the same endpoint and do opposite things with it. `sync`
leaves the ledger alone and reports the difference; `import` closes it. Use `sync`
when the ledger is meant to be complete and you want to know if it is. Use `import`
when it is knowingly incomplete — the month before you installed this, or a stretch
you forgot to log.

The local ledger is always the source of truth. `sync` adds GitHub's own count next to
it so you can see drift — requests you forgot to log, or logs that overstate.

```bash
# Personal account
ccred config set github.scope personal
ccred sync

# Organization
ccred config set github.scope organization
ccred config set github.org acme
ccred sync

# Enterprise, incl. GitHub Enterprise Server
ccred config set github.scope enterprise
ccred config set github.enterprise acme-inc
ccred config set github.apiBase https://ghe.acme.example/api/v3
ccred sync
```

Authentication comes from `CCRED_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, or
`gh auth token` — in that order. The token needs read access to billing ("Plan").
**Tokens are never written to disk by this tool.**

`ccred sync --dry-run` prints the exact URLs it would call and makes no network
requests at all.

A cycle anchored mid-month spans two calendar months; sync fetches both and filters
the line items down to your actual cycle window.

Caveats worth knowing before you trust the drift number:

- The billing usage endpoints require GitHub's enhanced billing platform. Older
  accounts and some GHES versions do not expose them, and sync will say so rather
  than guess.
- Sync is a reconciliation, not a replacement. Nothing in GitHub's report says *which
  prompt* a request belonged to, so session shape, prompt length and per-model
  efficiency can only come from the local ledger. The same limit applies to `import`,
  which is why backfilled entries are kept out of those numbers.
- The quantity GitHub reports is read as already-billed premium requests, so a day of
  Opus billed at 30 becomes 30 credits and 3 requests. If your report counts raw
  interactions instead, pass `--quantity raw`.
- Both commands accept a cycle id, and both write to that cycle's archive rather than
  the live ledger when it is a finished one.

## Model multipliers

`data/models.json` carries a multiplier table stamped with the date it was accurate
(`asOf`). **GitHub changes these.** Verify against their premium-request documentation
and correct anything stale — corrections are stored in your data directory and survive
upgrades:

```bash
ccred models --set claude-opus-4.1=10
ccred models --set some-new-model=2 --label "Some New Model"
```

Unknown models can also be registered inline the first time you log one:

```bash
ccred log some-new-model "trying it out" --multiplier 2
```

## Development

```bash
npm test          # node:test, no test framework to install
```

Tests cover the cycle maths (including reset-day 31 through February), rollover and
archiving, the metrics engine, argument parsing, the sync helpers, and the backfill —
CSV reading, SKU-to-model matching, gap filling, idempotency, and the guarantee that
imported spend never reaches the session-shape numbers.

```
src/core/     period maths, ledger, state + rollover, metrics, backfill,
              copilot.js - reading the CLI's local session logs
src/commands/ one file per command
src/util/     argv parsing, terminal formatting, text measurement, csv reading
data/         bundled multiplier table (legacy premium-request unit only)
```

`src/index.js` exposes the same pieces programmatically if you want to feed the data
somewhere else.

usage from the Copilot CLI instead of asking GitHub's billing API

The billing API was the wrong place to ask. It is an owner / billing-manager
surface, so the seat holder who wants this tool is the one most likely to be
refused - and the previous two commits answered that by building workarounds
around the wall rather than noticing the data was already local.

The Copilot CLI records what every session cost, on this machine, in
~/.copilot/session-state/<id>/events.jsonl. Its session.shutdown event
carries totalNanoAiu, totalPremiumRequests, the token counts and per-model
metrics. `ccred harvest` reads it: no token, no network, no billing
permission, nothing to configure.

It is also strictly more than billing returns. Billing gives a daily
quantity per SKU. This gives real token counts, AI credits, real session
start and end times, the model, the git branch and the lines changed.
Sessions are keyed by the CLI's own id, so harvesting is idempotent and
picks up whatever has run since last time.

Two things it deliberately refuses to do. A session that never shut down
cleanly is skipped rather than half-counted, and a session whose event
stream does not record its turns reports `turns: null` rather than 1 - a
multi-turn session logged as one prompt would quietly inflate the
one-and-done rate, which is the statistic this tool exists to report
honestly. Turns are counted when the events do record them.

Also corrects the billing model. `copilot help billing` states that usage
is measured in AI credits and that premium requests are the legacy
platform, and that per-token pricing replaced the per-model multiplier.
AI credits are now carried as a first-class unit through the ledger and
metrics (burn.aiu, burn.aiuPerDay, per-model aiu) alongside the legacy
premium-request count; neither is derived from the other, and an entry
from a source that reported only one does not get a fabricated value for
the other. The multiplier table is documented as legacy-only.

Ledger origins generalised: `isDerived` now covers both backfills and
harvested sessions, so anything the tool worked out rather than watched
stays out of session-shape statistics.

Verified against a live Copilot CLI 1.0.81 by capturing the statusLine
JSON payload, then removed the probe and left ~/.copilot as found. Field
reads are defensive throughout, so a CLI that changes shape harvests
nothing rather than writing wrong numbers.

84 tests pass (11 new), covering the nano-AIU conversion, shutdown parsing,
the refusal to guess turn counts, a half-written final line, lenient
per-model metrics, and an absent Copilot CLI.

enterprise-restricted users a way in

Billing usage is an owner / billing-manager surface, so a developer holding
a Copilot Business or Enterprise seat - exactly the person who wants this
tool - is the one most likely to get a 403 from it. That message was the
only failure with no way forward: 404 pointed at `--file`, 403 just said
"your org restricts it" and stopped.

Two changes so being blocked never means starting from zero.

`ccred import --credits 142` enters a total by hand, for the case where the
number can be read off a screen but not exported. `--credits opus=60,
sonnet=33` splits it by model when that is known. Model names go through
`resolveModel`, so a typo gets the usual "did you mean" instead of landing
silently as unattributed.

A hand-entered figure is an opening balance, not a day's work. It is dated
to the first day of the cycle and excluded from the busiest-day comparison,
which it would otherwise win every time without meaning anything by it. It
still counts toward budget, pace and projection - the point is that the
allowance is being spent either way. The existing gap arithmetic makes
re-checking natural: --credits 160 after 142 adds 18, and the same number
twice adds nothing.

Both restricted-access failures (403 and 404) now name the file route and
the manual route, as does the no-token error.

Also fixes an attribution bug found on the way: an explicit model column
went through the loose SKU matcher, which ignores keys under four
characters, so a row naming `o3` landed as unattributed. An exact model-id
match now wins outright.

73 tests pass (9 new), covering the opening-balance semantics, busiest-day
exclusion, re-entry arithmetic, credit-spec parsing, exact-id matching, and
that both failure messages name a route needing no API access.

`ccred import` so the tracker can start mid-cycle

The tool was forward-only: install it on the 20th and the first thing you
saw was an empty bar, with everything already spent that month invisible.
`sync` fetched GitHub's billing usage but only stored it as a comparison
blob, so the ledger stayed at zero next to "GitHub reported 96 requests".

`ccred import` turns that data into real ledger entries, from the billing
API or from a usage report downloaded from the web UI (CSV or JSON). The
file path matters: any account without the enhanced billing platform gets
a 404 from the API, and GHES may not expose it at all, so the failure now
points straight at `--file`.

Three things keep the numbers honest:

- Import fills the gap rather than appending. For each day and model it
  compares GitHub's number against what the ledger already holds and adds
  only the difference, so re-running is a no-op, hand-logged prompts are
  never double-counted, and logging more than GitHub reports leaves the
  ledger alone and surfaces the excess as drift.
- Imported entries are marked `origin: 'import'` and stay out of session
  shape, re-prompt tax, prompt length and credits-per-session. Billing
  data is a date, a SKU and a quantity - it cannot say which prompts
  belonged together, so it must not be allowed to invent a habit. It does
  count toward credits, pace, projection, daily burn and per-model spend.
- The quantity is read as already-billed premium requests, matching what
  `sync` compares against; `--quantity raw` covers a report that counts
  raw interactions instead.

GitHub reports no token counts in billing usage, so imported entries carry
credits and requests but never tokens, and the output says so rather than
showing a misleading zero. Token columns are carried across when a source
happens to have them.

Also here: the GitHub fetch plumbing is extracted from sync.js so both
commands share it, `init --import` pulls the cycle in during setup, the
empty-state hint points at import, and status/report/history/export show
what came from a backfill.

64 tests pass (27 new), covering CSV edge cases, longest-match SKU-to-model
inference, local-noon date pinning, gap arithmetic, idempotency, --replace,
and the guarantee that imported spend never reaches the session-shape
numbers.

commit: ccred, a Copilot credit efficiency tracker

Tracks GitHub Copilot premium-request credits per model and reports on
where they went, not just how many were spent.

- Burn rate against the plan allowance: pace, projection, safe daily
  budget, and the date the allowance runs out at the current rate.
- Session shape: one-prompt wins vs multi-prompt grinds, and the share
  of spend that went to follow-ups rather than openers.
- Per-model efficiency measured as credits per finished session, counted
  only over sessions run entirely on that model.
- Prompt length bucketed by opener, against the follow-ups it bought.
- Input / output / context tokens tracked separately, and priced
  separately when an agreement bills on tokens.

State lives outside the repo (APPDATA / Application Support / XDG, or
CCRED_HOME) so it persists across shells and sessions. Cycles roll over
automatically on the first command after the reset day: the finished
cycle is archived intact, open sessions are closed at the boundary, and
several missed cycles catch up in one pass.

Optional `ccred sync` reconciles the ledger against GitHub's billing
usage API for personal, organization or enterprise scopes, including
GHES base URLs. Tokens are read from the environment or gh and never
written to disk.

Zero runtime dependencies - Node built-ins only.

# twiceMeasured

A from-scratch toolchain for Power BI semantic models. No ADOMD.NET, no AMO/TOM,
no MSAL, no Tabular Editor, no DAX Studio. Just documented protocols spoken
directly.

The goal is a single tool that covers what Tabular Editor, DAX Studio, ALM
Toolkit, and the Power BI bits of Azure CLI cover today — with a typed API
surface an LLM agent can drive, rather than a GUI a human has to click.

## Status

Slices 1–7 complete: **auth + XMLA**, **VertiPaq analyzer**, **TMSL write path**,
**TMDL + model graph**, **diff + BPA**, **MCP server**, **DAX parser + formatter**.

| Raw OAuth2 (device code, client credentials, refresh) | MSAL | Done |
| Token cache | — | Done |
| XMLA SOAP transport, redirect-safe | ADOMD.NET transport | Done |

| DAX / DMV / Discover / TMSL execution | DAX Studio query pane | Done |
| DMV catalog + capability probe | — | Done |

## Cloud environments

Every endpoint the toolchain uses is configuration, not a literal: the OAuth2
authority, the token audience, the XMLA/REST host, the Fabric host, and the
allowlist of hosts permitted to receive the bearer token.

```bash
export TM_CLOUD=usgov          # commercial (default), usgov, china
```

Any field can be overridden on its own, which is what a private gateway or an
unusual tenant needs:

```bash
export TM_REGION_HOST=gateway.contoso.example
export TM_TOKEN_HOSTS=.contoso.example
```

| Variable | Sets |
|---|---|
| `TM_CLOUD` | Preset name or alias (`public`, `gcchigh`, `mooncake`, …) |
| `TM_AUTHORITY` | OAuth2 authority root |
| `TM_POWERBI_RESOURCE` | Token audience, which drives the `.default` scope |
| `TM_REGION_HOST` | XMLA and Power BI REST host |
| `TM_FABRIC_HOST` | Fabric REST host |
| `TM_TOKEN_HOSTS` | Comma-separated bearer-token allowlist |

Only `commercial` is confirmed against a live tenant. `usgov` and `china` are
assembled from published endpoint lists and report `verified: false`; overriding
any field marks the environment `+custom` and unverified too, so `server_info`
always shows whether you are on known ground.

## Prerequisites

### 1. Capacity

The XMLA endpoint requires **Premium, PPU, or a Fabric F-SKU**. A Pro-only
workspace exposes no XMLA endpoint at all and nothing here will connect.

In the Fabric/Power BI admin portal:

- **Capacity settings → Semantic models → XMLA Endpoint** — set to `Read Write`
- **Tenant settings → Allow XMLA endpoints and Analyze in Excel with
  on-premises datasets** — enabled

### 2. Entra app registration

You need your own app. These tools are not privileged; they authenticate exactly
the way your app will.

1. Entra admin center → **App registrations** → **New registration**
2. Name it, choose **Accounts in this organizational directory only**
3. Register. Note the **Application (client) ID** and **Directory (tenant) ID**
4. **Authentication → Advanced settings → Allow public client flows → Yes**
   *(required for device code sign-in; without it login fails with an
   unhelpful `invalid_client`)*
5. **API permissions → Add → Power BI Service → Delegated**, then add what you
   need — `Dataset.ReadWrite.All`, `Workspace.Read.All` are a reasonable start
6. **Grant admin consent**

The XMLA endpoint authorizes against your **workspace role**, not against these
scopes — the scopes matter for the REST APIs coming in a later slice. You still
need at least **Contributor** on the target workspace.

### 3. Service principal (optional, for automation)

Add a client secret to the app, then:

- **Tenant settings → Service principals can use Power BI APIs** — enabled
  (optionally scoped to a security group your SPN belongs to)
- Add the SPN to the target workspace as **Contributor** or higher

## Install

```bash
python -m venv .venv && ./.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
```

## Configure

Non-secret settings go to `~/.twicemeasured/config.json`:

```bash
tm configure --tenant-id <TENANT_GUID> --client-id <CLIENT_GUID> --workspace "My Workspace"
```

Anything can be overridden by environment variable — `TM_TENANT_ID`,
`TM_CLIENT_ID`, `TM_WORKSPACE`, `TM_DATABASE`. Secrets only ever come from the
environment:

```bash
export TM_CLIENT_SECRET=<SECRET>
```

Setting `TM_CLIENT_SECRET` switches auth from interactive device code to service
principal automatically.

## Use

```bash
tm login
```

```bash
tm ping --workspace "My Workspace"
```

```bash
tm catalogs --workspace "My Workspace"
```

```bash
tm dax 'EVALUATE TOPN(10, Sales)' --workspace "My Workspace" --database "Sales Model"
```

```bash
tm dmv 'SELECT * FROM $SYSTEM.DISCOVER_STORAGE_TABLE_COLUMN_SEGMENTS' -w "My Workspace" -d "Sales Model" --json
```

`tm rowsets` lists every Discover request type your endpoint actually supports,
and `tm probe` reports which DMVs it serves — both useful for establishing what
a given capacity exposes before building on it.

Both `dax` and `dmv` accept `-` to read the statement from stdin.

### VertiPaq analysis

```bash
tm vpa -w "My Workspace" -d "Sales Model"
```

Ranked tables and columns, with size split into data, dictionary, and hierarchy.
`--table Sales` drills into one table; `--json` emits the full metrics tree;
`--skip-dependencies` trades unreferenced-column detection for speed.

```bash
tm findings -w "My Workspace" -d "Sales Model" --severity warning
```

Actionable observations ranked by severity then by estimated bytes recovered.

### Refresh and deploy

Write commands preview by default and require `--yes` to fire:

```bash
tm refresh -d "Sales Model" --tables Orders --type dataOnly --show-command
```

```bash
tm refresh -d "Sales Model" --tables Orders Customer --staged --yes
```

`--staged` refreshes each table `dataOnly` then runs one `calculate`, which is
how you refresh a model too large to fit a full refresh in memory.

```bash
tm deploy model.json -d "Sales Model" --yes
```

`tm tmsl commands.json` runs raw TMSL through the same confirmation gate.

### Model files

Everything under `tm model` is offline — it reads TMDL folders and needs no
endpoint at all.

```bash
tm model summary ./MyModel.SemanticModel/definition
```

```bash
tm model deps ./definition
```

```bash
tm model unused ./definition
```

```bash
tm model check ./definition
```

`check` reports circular dependencies and exits non-zero when it finds any,
so it works as a CI gate.

```bash
tm model tmsl ./definition -d "Sales Model" -o model.json
```

`tm model tmsl` closes the loop: TMDL folder -> model graph -> TMSL definition,
which `tm deploy model.json` then pushes.

### Compare and review

```bash
tm diff ./dev/definition ./prod/definition --plan
```

Source is the desired state, target is what is deployed -- so an object only in
source is a *create*. `--plan` adds how it would deploy; `-o deploy.json` writes
the deployment TMSL; `--allow-deletes` lets the plan drop tables missing from
source, which it will not do otherwise.

```bash
tm bpa ./definition --severity warning
```

```bash
tm bpa ./definition --disable calculated-column visible-key-column
```

Both take `--exit-code` for CI: `diff` exits 1 when anything differs, `bpa` exits
1 on any error-severity violation.
